cards.title: Australia’s Refusal to Repatriate IS Families Turns Counterterrorism Into a Citizenship Test
cards.background: Four Australian women linked to Islamic State returned from Syria to Australia this week, after years detained in the Al-Roj camp; three were swiftly arrested and one remained under scrutiny. Australia has resisted repatriating dozens of its citizens from Syrian camps for years, despite legal rights of return and repeated pressure from advocates. The issue has become more politically charged after a December mass shooting at a Jewish event in Bondi Beach that killed 15 people and was allegedly inspired by IS. Twenty-one Australians remain in Al-Roj, including seven women and 14 children.

prop_args.thesis: Australia should repatriate IS-linked women and children because keeping them in Syrian camps is both less secure and less just than bringing them home under law-enforcement control.
mechanisms: First, repatriation improves security management. This is because (1) Australian authorities can monitor, arrest, and prosecute returnees under domestic law, (2) Syrian camps like Al-Roj are described as incubators for radicalisation and violence, and (3) indefinite detention in a collapsing camp environment leaves states with no real oversight while the risk profile worsens.

Second, repatriation protects children from becoming a second generation of extremists. Three reasons: one, many of the children have never lived outside the camps and are being socialised in a closed, trauma-heavy environment; two, the longer they remain, the more entrenched their psychological, educational, and ideological deprivation becomes; three, Australia can pair return with integration and countering violent extremism programmes, giving a better chance of de-radicalisation than abandonment in Syria.

Third, the rule-of-law and citizenship principles are stronger on the prop side. This matters because (1) citizens have a legal right to return, (2) punishing children for the alleged crimes of their parents creates collective punishment logic, and (3) if the state can selectively deny return based on public anger, it sets a dangerous precedent that political fear overrides legal rights.

opp_args.thesis: Australia should block or minimise repatriation because returning IS-linked families creates immediate domestic security, political, and social harms that outweigh abstract legal duties.
mechanisms: First, return can create a direct security risk. One, some returnees may still be ideologically committed or capable of facilitating extremist networks; two, intelligence on individuals from Syrian camps is often incomplete, making risk assessment unreliable; three, even a small number of failures has catastrophic downside in a country already traumatised by an IS-inspired attack.

Second, repatriation imposes severe social and political costs. One, survivors of IS atrocities, especially Yazidi refugees and other victims, may experience renewed trauma and fear encountering returnees; two, public trust in government drops when leaders appear to prioritise suspected extremists over victims; three, the backlash can strengthen anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim politics, making the broader social environment less stable.

Third, refusing return is a deterrence and responsibility signal. One, it tells would-be foreign fighters and their families that joining a terrorist entity has lasting consequences; two, it reduces incentives for future radical travel by making state rescue less likely; three, it avoids rewarding choices that were made voluntarily, or at least perceived by the public as voluntary, which is politically important for maintaining legitimacy.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term domestic risk and long-term state control. Prop wins if the judge prioritises actual manageability: once people are home, the state can arrest, monitor, and rehabilitate them, whereas leaving them in Al-Roj only externalises the problem and worsens children’s outcomes. Opp wins if the judge thinks one serious security failure or victim-trauma event outweighs the benefits of legal consistency.

THBT states should not strip or effectively abandon the citizenship of women and children associated with ISIS fighters
THP a world in which governments are legally required to repatriate nationals from foreign detention camps
TH, as a counterterrorism agency, would prioritise rehabilitation over permanent exclusion for low-level terror affiliates

cards.title: Iran’s Hormuz Leverage Turns a Ceasefire Into a Global Economic Hostage Crisis
cards.region: Iran / Strait of Hormuz / Middle East / Global
cards.background: On 8 May 2026, Bloomberg reported that the US expected Iran to respond imminently to its latest proposal to end the war, while clashes in the Strait of Hormuz threatened to fracture a monthlong ceasefire. The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints, carrying a large share of globally traded oil and liquefied natural gas. The article frames the situation as both a military standoff and an economic pressure point, with any escalation immediately affecting global markets and regional security.

prop_args.thesis: Iran’s control over Hormuz gives it disproportionate leverage over the global economy, making coercion and escalation more effective than conventional battlefield gains.
mechanisms: First, Hormuz creates a chokepoint veto over energy flows. This is because (1) a large share of seaborne oil and LNG must pass through the strait, (2) even short-lived disruption raises insurance, freight, and futures prices immediately, and (3) markets price in risk faster than states can physically reroute supply.

Second, Iran can weaponize uncertainty without needing full closure. Three reasons: one, intermittent harassment of shipping is cheaper than sustained war; two, ambiguity forces firms and states to overreact through precautionary stockpiling and rerouting; three, the economic pain is global while the military cost is concentrated and manageable for Iran.

Third, this leverage translates into diplomatic bargaining power. This matters because the threat to energy markets pressures import-dependent states, splits coalition unity, and gives Iran a way to extract concessions even when it cannot win a conventional war.

opp_args.thesis: Hormuz is a powerful pressure point, but it is not an unlimited trump card because Iran’s own economy and military position make prolonged disruption self-defeating.
mechanisms: First, escalation through Hormuz imposes severe blowback on Iran itself. One, Iran also depends on regional trade, smuggling routes, and stable oil revenue; two, prolonged conflict invites harsher sanctions, interdiction, and retaliation; three, any spike in global prices can accelerate international coordination against Tehran.

Second, the world has adapted to Hormuz risk better than before. One, states maintain strategic petroleum reserves and diversified supply chains; two, producers outside the Gulf can partially offset shocks over time; three, shipping and naval protection reduce the chance that Iran can sustain a total blockade.

Third, coercion through chokepoints is limited because it is hard to control outcomes. One, markets may absorb short disruptions without forcing political concessions; two, allies and rivals may harden rather than compromise; three, if Iran overplays its hand, it risks turning a bargaining chip into a casus belli.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether leverage requires durable control or just the credible threat of disruption. Prop wins if the round is about immediate economic vulnerability and bargaining power; opp wins if the round is about sustainability, because Iran’s leverage is strongest precisely when it is not fully used.

THBT states should treat control of maritime chokepoints as a form of economic warfare
THP a world where regional powers can credibly threaten global shipping lanes to gain diplomatic leverage

cards.title: Trump-Backed Mini-Ceasefire Exposes How Fragile Russia-Ukraine De-escalation Has Become
cards.background: Donald Trump announced a three-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, saying it would include a suspension of all kinetic activity and a prisoner swap of 1,000 prisoners from each side. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed participation, and Russian state media said Moscow had agreed, after both sides had accused each other of violating earlier ceasefires tied to Victory Day celebrations on 8-9 May. The Kremlin had separately warned of a 'retaliatory, massive missile strike' if Kyiv attacked the Red Square parade, while Moscow said around 20 drones were downed near the city and Ukraine said it faced more than 140 attacks and 850 drone strikes in the first hours of the truce.

prop_args.thesis: Even a short, externally mediated ceasefire is valuable because it creates a rare off-ramp from escalation, saves lives immediately, and can build the minimum trust needed for future negotiations.
mechanisms: First, it reduces immediate battlefield and civilian harm. This is because (1) a formal pause lowers the tempo of artillery, drone, and missile exchanges; (2) even a 72-hour window can prevent hundreds of deaths and injuries in a war where both sides are actively striking cities and infrastructure; (3) the prisoner swap adds a concrete humanitarian gain that is politically easier to sustain than a full peace deal.

Second, it creates a testing ground for compliance and communication. Three reasons: one, both sides can observe whether the other is capable of enforcing orders across fragmented fronts; two, third-party mediation by the US gives each side a channel to deconflict without conceding core war aims; three, repeated short truces can gradually normalize negotiation and reduce the 'no talks until victory' mindset.

Third, it improves the strategic environment for later diplomacy. This matters because a temporary pause can reduce pressure on Europe and the US to choose between escalation and abandonment, while also showing that limited agreements are possible even when final-status peace is not.

opp_args.thesis: A three-day ceasefire is mostly performative and can worsen the war by giving both sides propaganda cover, operational intelligence, and a false sense that diplomacy is progressing when the underlying conflict is unchanged.
mechanisms: First, it is easy to violate and therefore easy to weaponize politically. One, both Russia and Ukraine are already accusing each other of breaches within hours, so each side can claim the other is the aggressor; two, because the ceasefire is so short, any violation becomes a pretext to resume escalation immediately; three, the public spectacle around Victory Day turns the truce into messaging rather than genuine de-escalation.

Second, it can create military asymmetry rather than peace. One, pauses allow both sides to reposition, resupply, repair air defenses, and assess the other's capabilities; two, the side with better command-and-control or drone reconnaissance can exploit the lull more effectively; three, if one side believes the other is using the pause to prepare a strike, it may preemptively harden or escalate after the ceasefire ends.

Third, it distracts from the real diplomatic problem: there is no settlement architecture. One, the war has already seen multiple failed mediation rounds without breakthrough; two, a symbolic pause lets external actors claim progress without addressing territory, security guarantees, or sanctions; three, it can reduce pressure for serious negotiations by substituting headlines for substance.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether temporary de-escalation has independent value even when it does not solve the war. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes immediate lives saved and sees diplomacy as a ladder of small steps; opp wins if they show the truce is too short and too politicized to change incentives, making it more likely to be exploited than to produce durable peace.

cards.title: Libya’s Oil Infrastructure Becomes a Battlefield, Exposing the State’s Loss of Monopoly on Force
cards.background: Libya’s largest operational refinery at Zawiya, about 40km west of Tripoli, was shut down on 8 May 2026 after armed clashes erupted nearby. The National Oil Corporation and Zawiya Refining Company declared a “precautionary halt,” evacuated workers, and said emergency sirens were activated after heavy weapons projectiles landed inside the oil complex. The refinery has a capacity of 120,000 barrels per day and is linked to the 300,000 bpd Sharara oilfield. Since the 2011 fall of Muammar Gaddafi, Libya has remained split between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and the eastern-based forces aligned with Khalifa Haftar.

prop_args.thesis: This shutdown shows why fragmented states cannot safely manage strategic energy assets: once armed groups can threaten refineries, the state loses both revenue and coercive control.
mechanisms: First, the halt directly weakens state capacity by interrupting oil throughput and forcing emergency closures. This is because (1) Libya’s fiscal system depends heavily on hydrocarbons, (2) even a precautionary shutdown reduces export reliability and domestic fuel planning, and (3) repeated disruptions make the state look incapable of protecting its own economic backbone.

Second, it empowers armed actors by turning infrastructure into leverage. Three reasons: one, groups that can threaten a refinery can extract concessions from local authorities; two, they can use disruption to signal territorial control and deter rivals; three, the more the state negotiates around these actors, the more it normalizes parallel power structures.

Third, it increases the risk of broader conflict escalation and regional spillover. This matters because a refinery adjacent to residential areas and connected to major oil production creates a high-value target; any serious damage would hit fuel supply, raise domestic instability, and threaten Mediterranean energy markets that already fear Libyan supply shocks.

opp_args.thesis: The shutdown is a short-term precaution, not proof of systemic collapse, and it shows that Libya still has institutions capable of protecting critical infrastructure and restoring output.
mechanisms: First, the response demonstrates residual state and corporate capacity. One, the NOC and refinery management evacuated staff quickly, preventing casualties; two, they publicly coordinated an emergency halt rather than allowing uncontrolled damage; three, they stated fuel supplies would continue as normal, limiting immediate economic harm.

Second, the incident may actually justify stronger security operations against armed groups. One, authorities framed the fighting as targeting criminal networks involved in kidnapping, extortion, trafficking, and illegal migration; two, that gives the government a legitimate basis to clear predatory actors from strategic zones; three, if successful, this can improve long-term security around energy infrastructure.

Third, Libya’s oil sector has historically been resilient despite political fragmentation. One, the refinery itself was not reported to have suffered significant damage; two, the shutdown was precautionary rather than a destruction event; three, once the area stabilizes, production can restart relatively quickly, meaning the strategic impact may be temporary rather than transformative.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether one sees the incident as a symptom of irreversible state failure or a temporary security disruption. Prop wins if it proves that repeated threats to oil infrastructure structurally weaken sovereignty and revenue; Opp wins if it frames the event as a contained, reversible interruption with institutions still functioning.

cards.title: New York’s Pied-à-Terre Tax Exposes the Limits of Taxing Wealth Without Driving Capital Flight
cards.region: United States (New York City; New York State)
cards.background: On 2026-05-08, Bloomberg reported that New York officials were still trying to design Governor Kathy Hochul’s proposed pied-à-terre tax, a levy aimed at taxing non-primary residences in New York City. The report said major questions about how the tax would work remained unresolved, and that the issue was feeding broader Democratic discord over the state budget. The proposal has already angered wealthy property owners and is being discussed in the context of New York’s wider fiscal politics.

prop_args.thesis: A well-designed pied-à-terre tax is a legitimate way to raise progressive revenue from luxury real estate without materially harming ordinary New Yorkers.
mechanisms: First, it targets a narrow, high-ability-to-pay base rather than broad consumption or payroll. This is because (1) second-home owners are disproportionately wealthy and can absorb a modest levy, (2) the tax can be structured to hit only high-value non-primary residences, and (3) it avoids raising taxes on renters and middle-income homeowners who are more price-sensitive.

Second, it improves allocative efficiency by discouraging underused speculative housing demand. Three reasons: one, luxury apartments held as stores of wealth sit vacant or lightly used, two, taxing them raises the carrying cost of speculation, and three, that nudges capital toward productive investment or owner-occupied housing.

Third, it can help stabilize state finances and reduce reliance on regressive revenue tools. This matters because (1) New York faces recurring budget pressure, (2) progressive property taxation is harder to evade than income shifting for some high-net-worth actors, and (3) earmarking or visibly linking the tax to public services increases legitimacy for the broader tax system.

opp_args.thesis: The pied-à-terre tax is politically attractive but economically and administratively fragile, so it is likely to underperform or backfire.
mechanisms: First, the tax is hard to design and enforce without creating loopholes and litigation. One, defining 'primary residence' versus 'pied-à-terre' is administratively messy, two, wealthy owners can restructure ownership through trusts, LLCs, or residency claims, and three, complexity raises compliance costs that eat into revenue.

Second, it risks capital flight and reduced high-end investment in New York real estate. One, mobile wealthy buyers can shift purchases to Miami, Florida, or other low-tax jurisdictions, two, luxury property markets depend on a small number of marginal buyers so even a modest tax can change behavior, and three, lower demand can weaken construction, brokerage, and related service sectors.

Third, it may intensify intra-party conflict and reduce the chance of coherent fiscal reform. One, Democrats are already split over the state budget, two, a controversial tax can become a bargaining chip that crowds out broader reforms, and three, symbolic taxes on the rich can substitute for more durable but politically harder revenue solutions.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between symbolic fairness and actual fiscal yield. Proponents win if they prove the tax is narrow, enforceable, and revenue-positive; opponents win if they show that complexity and avoidance make the policy more politics than policy, with the structural advantage on the opposition because high-end taxpayers are unusually mobile and legally sophisticated.

THBT cities should tax underused luxury housing to fund public services
THP a world where wealthy non-residents are heavily taxed for owning urban property

cards.title: Mystery Sea Drone in Greek Waters Raises Stakes in the Ukraine-Russia Maritime Shadow War
cards.region: Greece / Ionian Sea / Ukraine-Russia conflict spillover
cards.background: Greek authorities are investigating an unmanned naval drone found by fishermen in a cave near Lefkada in the Ionian Sea on Thursday, before the coast guard towed it to the port of Vasiliki. Greek media reported that the drone may have carried explosives and that its engine was still running when discovered. Officials have not confirmed its origin, but reports suggest it could be Ukrainian-made or linked to the Russia-Ukraine war; some Greek reporting says it resembles Ukraine's MAGURA V5 sea drone. The incident comes amid wider use of sea drones in the Black Sea and beyond, including reported attacks on Russian shipping and a March accusation by Moscow that Ukraine struck a sanctioned tanker in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta.

prop_args.thesis: The spread of naval drones into the Mediterranean makes maritime conflict harder to contain and pushes neutral states like Greece into the frontline of the Ukraine-Russia war.
mechanisms: First, this expands the geographic scope of the conflict. One, sea drones can travel far beyond traditional battle zones, meaning attacks are no longer confined to the Black Sea. Two, once a drone is found in Greek waters, every coastal state in the Mediterranean has to treat its own ports, shipping lanes, and infrastructure as potential targets. Three, that forces neutral or semi-neutral states to invest in surveillance, interception, and port security even if they are not formal belligerents.

Second, it increases escalation risk through attribution problems. One, the drone had no visible markings and its origin is still unclear, so states may misread accidents or technical failures as deliberate attacks. Two, if a drone is linked to Ukraine, Russia can frame this as proof that Kyiv is internationalising the war and justify retaliation against shipping or third states. Three, if it is linked to Russia or a false-flag operation, the same ambiguity can be used to widen the conflict diplomatically and militarily.

Third, it normalises asymmetric maritime warfare against commercial shipping. One, the article notes that sea drones have already been used against Russian warships and tankers, including sanctioned vessels tied to the shadow fleet. Two, once this tactic proves effective, states and proxies have incentives to target civilian-adjacent maritime infrastructure because it is cheaper than conventional naval power. Three, that raises insurance costs, disrupts trade routes, and makes the Mediterranean a more militarised commons.

opp_args.thesis: This incident is more likely a contained technical mishap than a major escalation, so it should not be overread as proof of broader regional destabilisation.
mechanisms: First, the evidence for intentional spillover is weak. One, the drone was found with no visible markings and officials have not confirmed its origin. Two, Greek military experts are explicitly considering technical failure or loss of communications with the control centre. Three, without attribution, the case is a single unexplained object rather than proof of a systematic campaign.

Second, even if it is Ukrainian-linked, the strategic effect may be limited. One, Ukraine has strong incentives to use cheap naval drones against Russian shipping because they are cost-effective and avoid direct conventional confrontation. Two, targeting the shadow fleet is aimed at sanction enforcement and military pressure, not at opening a new front against Greece or the EU. Three, states can absorb isolated incidents through coast guard and intelligence coordination without broader escalation.

Third, this may actually strengthen deterrence and maritime security rather than undermine it. One, the discovery shows that coastal states can detect, recover, and investigate such systems before they cause harm. Two, public exposure of the drone can improve monitoring of suspicious maritime activity and force better port security. Three, if the incident is treated as a law-enforcement and intelligence issue, it can be contained below the threshold of interstate conflict.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether one recovered drone is evidence of a new maritime security regime or just an isolated spillover event. Prop wins if the round is about precedent and attribution risk, because even one ambiguous incident forces neutral states to reprice the entire Mediterranean as a conflict zone; opp wins if the round is about material impact, because the current facts still point to a single recoverable object with uncertain origin.
motion_areas: TH, as Greece, would treat unidentified naval drones in its waters as acts of war
THBT European states should expand military support to Ukraine despite spillover risks to Mediterranean security
THP a world where states are allowed to target shadow fleet shipping with autonomous sea drones

cards.title: Trump FCC Uses Equal-Time Rules to Pressure ABC, Raising Fears of Regulatory Retaliation Against Critical Media
cards.background: On 7 May 2026, ABC-owned KTRK-TV filed a legal motion against an FCC enforcement action over The View, after FCC chair Brendan Carr confirmed in February that the agency was investigating whether the show violated equal-time rules by featuring Texas Senate candidate James Talarico without giving all rivals equal access. ABC argues The View qualifies as a "bona fide" news interview program and is exempt from equal-time rules, while the FCC says it will review that claim. The dispute comes as the 2026 midterm election cycle approaches and as Disney, ABC’s parent company, is already facing a separate FCC investigation into its DEI practices and an order to seek early renewal of eight local station licenses.

prop_args.thesis: The FCC’s action is a politically motivated regulatory threat that chills broadcast speech and narrows voter access to political information.
mechanisms: First, selective enforcement creates a direct chilling effect on broadcasters. This is because (1) stations now face the risk that any candidate interview could trigger costly scrutiny, (2) editors will preemptively avoid controversial or politically salient guests to reduce legal exposure, and (3) the uncertainty is especially damaging on broadcast TV, where compliance burdens are higher than on cable, podcasts, or social media.

Second, the investigation weaponizes an old doctrine in a media environment where it is increasingly distortionary. Three reasons: one, broadcast airwaves are now only a small slice of political information channels, so forcing equal airtime does not meaningfully expand speech; two, it makes normal news programming infeasible because every candidate appearance can require balancing obligations; three, it privileges procedural compliance over editorial judgment, which is exactly what the First Amendment is meant to protect.

Third, the FCC’s broader pattern suggests retaliation rather than neutral rule enforcement. This matters because (1) the agency is simultaneously investigating Disney’s DEI practices, (2) it has already ordered ABC to seek early license renewal years ahead of schedule, and (3) that combination signals to other outlets that criticism of the administration can trigger regulatory pain, producing self-censorship across the industry.

opp_args.thesis: The FCC is legitimately enforcing a long-standing election-integrity rule that prevents broadcasters from giving unfair political advantages to favored candidates.
mechanisms: First, equal-time rules exist to stop broadcasters from using scarce public spectrum to tilt elections. One, broadcast licenses are public privileges, not private entitlements; two, the rule prevents networks from effectively endorsing candidates through selective access; three, requiring equal treatment increases electoral fairness by ensuring rival candidates can reach the same audience.

Second, The View may not clearly qualify for the bona fide news exemption, so review is appropriate. One, the show is a talk program with strong opinion content rather than a conventional news interview format; two, the FCC has a duty to test whether the exemption is being stretched beyond its intended scope; three, if the exemption is too broad, networks can evade equal-time obligations simply by labeling partisan commentary as journalism.

Third, the rule does not ban speech; it only conditions candidate access on neutrality. This matters because (1) ABC can still cover politics extensively through non-candidate commentary, (2) candidates can appear on many other platforms, and (3) the burden is limited to ensuring that one network does not become a campaign tool for one side.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the FCC is neutrally enforcing election law or using regulation to punish disfavored speech. Prop wins if you think the pattern of investigations and early license pressure creates a broader chilling effect across media; opp wins if you prioritize electoral fairness and accept that broadcast spectrum justifies stricter rules than cable or social media.

THBT regulators should not use licensing power to pressure media outlets critical of the government
THP a world where broadcast news programs are exempt from equal-time obligations
THBT governments should have broad authority to police political fairness on public airwaves

cards.title: Malaysia’s Rare Earth Hub Becomes a Battleground Over Military Supply Chains and Great-Power Alignment
cards.background: A coalition of 57 Malaysian civil society organizations issued a memorandum on April 14 opposing an approximately $96 million rare earths supply deal between Australia’s Lynas Corporation and the U.S. Department of Defense. The deal would reportedly involve Lynas processing rare earth materials at its Gebeng facility in Pahang for supply to the U.S. defense sector. The backlash comes as Malaysia is also facing broader trade uncertainty after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) were unconstitutional, undermining the Malaysia-U.S. Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) signed in October 2025.

prop_args.thesis: Malaysia should resist becoming a processing node in foreign military supply chains because the economic upside is outweighed by legal, reputational, and strategic costs.
mechanisms: First, the deal creates direct complicity risk. This is because (1) rare earth oxides are essential inputs in advanced weapons systems, (2) processing occurs on Malaysian soil under Malaysian licensing and regulatory approval, and (3) Article 16 of ARSIWA makes states liable if they knowingly aid another state’s internationally wrongful acts, so the government cannot plausibly claim neutrality once it authorizes the chain.

Second, it damages Malaysia’s foreign-policy brand as a non-aligned middle power. Three reasons: one, Malaysia has long claimed to oppose the use of force in international relations; two, being tied to U.S. defense procurement weakens its credibility when criticizing conflicts involving Palestine, Iran, or other flashpoints; three, reputational damage reduces Malaysia’s ability to act as an honest broker in ASEAN and multilateral forums.

Third, it increases long-run strategic vulnerability rather than resilience. This matters because the more Malaysia specializes in politically sensitive supply chains, the more it becomes exposed to coercion, sanctions risk, and domestic backlash, which can scare off broader investment and make future industrial policy harder to execute.

prop_args.thesis: Malaysia is better off using rare earths for domestic industrial upgrading than exporting strategic leverage to great powers.
mechanisms: First, domestic processing captures more value than raw or semi-processed export. This is because (1) rare earths are strategically important but Malaysia’s reserves are relatively modest, so the real gain is in downstream processing and capability-building, (2) local value-add supports jobs, skills, and industrial clustering, and (3) keeping the sector for domestic use prevents foreign actors from extracting the strategic rents.

Second, a domestic-first strategy reduces dependence on volatile external demand. Three reasons: one, U.S. tariff policy has become legally and politically unstable after the IEEPA ruling; two, firms are already delaying investment and procurement because of tariff unpredictability; three, a home-market anchor gives Malaysia a more predictable base for planning and financing.

Third, it strengthens bargaining power in a fragmented global economy. This matters because if Malaysia becomes indispensable in semiconductors, EV batteries, and other high-tech supply chains, it can raise the cost of coercion from both Washington and Beijing while preserving room for multi-alignment.

opp_args.thesis: Malaysia should allow the deal because integrating into trusted non-Chinese supply chains brings investment, industrial upgrading, and strategic diversification.
mechanisms: First, the deal helps Malaysia move up the value chain. One, rare earth processing is capital-intensive and technologically demanding, so foreign-linked contracts can transfer know-how; two, participation in defense-adjacent supply chains can attract higher-quality industrial investment; three, it helps Malaysia build credibility as a reliable processing hub outside China.

Second, refusing the deal risks leaving Malaysia stuck in low-value, politically irrelevant production. One, rare earth reserves are modest, so the country cannot rely on scale alone; two, if Malaysia over-prioritizes symbolism, it may miss the chance to monetize a scarce strategic asset; three, other states will simply capture the market if Malaysia hesitates.

Third, the backlash overstates legal exposure and underestimates state discretion. One, supplying processed materials is not the same as directly participating in military operations; two, ARSIWA complicity requires knowledge and a sufficiently proximate causal link, which governments can manage through licensing and compliance safeguards; three, clear regulation can preserve neutrality while still allowing commercial benefit.

opp_args.thesis: Malaysia should deepen economic ties with the U.S. and its partners because diversification away from China is a hedge against coercion.
mechanisms: First, the global supply chain environment is already weaponized. One, China has used rare earths as a geopolitical tool; two, U.S. trade policy is volatile but still offers access to a huge market and advanced technology; three, spreading exposure across multiple blocs reduces the risk that any single power can choke Malaysia’s exports.

Second, the economic cost of disengagement is immediate and concrete. One, exporters are already facing tariff uncertainty and cutting costs; two, businesses need stable external demand to sustain employment and investment; three, rejecting U.S.-linked opportunities could worsen uncertainty at a time when Malaysia is already exposed to trade fragmentation.

Third, strategic neutrality is more credible when backed by capability and partnerships. One, a country with no leverage is not truly neutral but merely vulnerable; two, participation in multiple frameworks like IPEF, RCEP, and defense-adjacent industrial networks increases Malaysia’s options; three, more options mean more autonomy in a great-power rivalry.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the rare earth deal is treated as a narrow commercial transaction or as a strategic alignment choice with legal and reputational spillovers. Prop wins if the round is about complicity, neutrality, and long-run sovereignty; Opp wins if the round is about industrial upgrading, hedging, and the reality that Malaysia cannot afford to sit out strategic supply chains.

cards.title: China’s Dual-Use Cyber Campaign Turns Espionage Into Transnational Repression Across Asia and NATO Space
cards.region: Pakistan; Thailand; Malaysia; India; Myanmar; Sri Lanka; Taiwan; Poland; broader Asia-Europe
cards.background: On May 1, Trend Micro disclosed Shadow-Earth-053, a China-aligned espionage campaign active since at least December 2024. It targeted government and defense networks in Pakistan, Thailand, Malaysia, India, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, and Poland, while also phishing Uyghur, Tibetan, Taiwanese, and Hong Kong critics plus journalists. The campaign used unpatched Microsoft Exchange and IIS servers, including ProxyLogon vulnerabilities, and separate phishing operations tracked as Glitter Carp and Sequin Carp began in April and June 2025. The article says nearly half the targets were also hit by Shadow-Earth-054, and notes a Dutch military intelligence assessment that China has reached parity with the United States in offensive cyber capability.

prop_args.thesis: China’s cyber operations are becoming a strategic threat multiplier because they combine intelligence collection with transnational repression, weakening both state security and democratic information ecosystems.
mechanisms: First, the campaign gives Beijing classic intelligence advantages against governments and defense ministries. This is because (1) access to ministries and contractors in countries like India, Taiwan, and Poland can reveal military planning, procurement, and alliance coordination; (2) compromising Exchange and IIS servers allows long-term persistence, so the intelligence yield compounds over time; and (3) targeting edge devices and servers creates broad access to internal networks rather than isolated files.

Second, the same infrastructure is used to silence diaspora critics and journalists. Three reasons: one, phishing with tracking pixels identifies when and where targets open messages, making surveillance and intimidation more precise; two, stealing credentials and tokens lets attackers monitor dissidents’ communications and source networks; three, by targeting exiled communities abroad, Beijing extends domestic censorship beyond its borders and deters future speech.

Third, this matters because it erodes alliance trust and the open information environment at the same time. This matters because (1) states become less willing to share sensitive data if they believe their networks are penetrated; (2) host governments face pressure to protect residents from foreign political policing, creating diplomatic friction with China; and (3) repeated exposure normalizes the idea that cyber coercion is a low-cost tool of statecraft, making deterrence harder.

opp_args.thesis: This campaign is serious, but it is not strategically transformative because most of the damage is limited to espionage and harassment rather than decisive coercion or physical disruption.
mechanisms: First, the operational effects are constrained by the nature of cyber espionage. One, stealing information does not automatically translate into battlefield advantage if the intelligence is stale, incomplete, or already compartmentalized; two, many governments rotate credentials and patch systems after disclosure, reducing long-term value; three, espionage campaigns are common enough that targets build institutional resilience and do not fundamentally alter foreign policy.

Second, transnational repression through phishing has limited reach compared with broader political control tools. One, only a subset of activists and journalists are vulnerable to targeted spearphishing; two, victims can migrate to encrypted platforms, burner accounts, and stronger operational security; three, the campaign’s effects are mostly chilling rather than eliminative, so opposition networks often adapt rather than collapse.

Third, the geopolitical response can absorb this without major escalation. One, NATO and Quad states already treat China as a persistent cyber threat, so disclosure reinforces existing threat models rather than creating a new one; two, sanctions or defensive coordination can raise costs without changing the overall balance of power; three, because cyber attribution is often deniable and incremental, Beijing can keep operating but also cannot convert these campaigns into durable coercive leverage.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether cyber operations are just another form of espionage or a durable tool of political control. Prop wins if the round is about cumulative erosion: repeated access, repression of diaspora voices, and alliance distrust create structural damage that is hard to reverse. Opp wins if the judge prioritizes immediacy and magnitude, because the article shows broad intrusion but not a decisive kinetic or economic shock.

THBT the Quad should treat cyber operations against diaspora communities as a core security threat
THP a world where states can retaliate economically for cyber-enabled political repression
TH, as democratic host states, would prioritize protection of exiled dissidents over diplomatic neutrality with China

cards.title: Trump’s Tariff Defeats Expose the Limits of Executive Trade Power in the U.S.
cards.background: On May 8, 2026, the U.S. Court of International Trade struck down Donald Trump’s latest 10 percent global tariff, which he had imposed earlier in the year after the Supreme Court had already invalidated a prior tariff effort. The ruling was the administration’s fifth judicial loss on its trade war, though the tariffs were not immediately eliminated for all parties and could remain in place until July while the White House prepares a new legal workaround. The case centered on Section 122 of the 1974 Trade Act, a statute originally designed to address the post-Nixon balance-of-payments problem and capped at 15 percent duties for 150 days.

prop_args.thesis: Courts striking down Trump’s tariffs is good because it restores constitutional checks on executive economic coercion and prevents arbitrary tax policy.
mechanisms: First, it reasserts that tariff-setting is effectively taxation and therefore belongs to Congress, not the president. This is because (1) tariffs raise prices on imports and function like a tax on consumers and firms, (2) letting one executive impose them unilaterally creates a de facto monarchy over fiscal policy, and (3) judicial review prevents presidents from laundering broad economic policy through emergency statutes.

Second, it reduces policy instability and the chilling effect on investment. Three reasons: one, firms cannot plan supply chains when duties can appear and disappear by proclamation; two, uncertainty raises hedging and compliance costs across sectors; three, repeated legal defeats signal that arbitrary tariffs are not durable, which discourages firms from overreacting to short-term political shocks.

Third, it protects the legitimacy of trade policy by forcing the government to use proper legislative channels. This matters because durable industrial policy needs clear rules, congressional buy-in, and predictable scope; otherwise trade becomes a tool of personalist politics rather than a coherent economic strategy.

opp_args.thesis: The court rulings are bad because they weaken the president’s ability to respond quickly to trade imbalances and foreign economic pressure.
mechanisms: First, they constrain emergency economic management. One, trade deficits and import surges can move faster than Congress can legislate; two, the executive is often the only actor able to respond in real time; three, if courts narrowly read old statutes, the U.S. loses flexibility to defend domestic industries during shocks.

Second, they encourage foreign free-riding and domestic paralysis. One, trading partners can wait out congressional gridlock knowing the president lacks unilateral tools; two, industries harmed by import competition receive delayed relief; three, the threat of tariffs is less credible, reducing U.S. leverage in negotiations.

Third, they may not eliminate tariffs in practice, only force legalistic workarounds. One, the administration can shift to other statutory authorities; two, repeated litigation creates uncertainty without solving the underlying trade dispute; three, the result is a more opaque and less accountable tariff regime rather than a cleaner one.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between constitutional constraint and economic responsiveness. Prop wins if the round is about rule of law and preventing arbitrary taxation; opp wins if the round prioritizes executive agility in a world of fast-moving trade shocks and congressional gridlock.

THBT Congress should reclaim tariff-setting authority from the executive branch
THP a world where presidents cannot unilaterally impose broad import tariffs

cards.title: U.S.-Israeli Strikes Trigger Rally-Around-the-Flag Politics in Tehran, Delaying Regime Collapse
cards.background: In a Foreign Policy interview published on 2026-05-08, reporter Ali Hashem described spending six weeks in Tehran during an ongoing war involving U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran. He said shops, restaurants, and malls in Tehran remained partly open, while many residents adapted to bombardment by moving between neighborhoods and using a state-linked domestic intranet with local versions of apps like WhatsApp, Uber, Netflix, and delivery services. Hashem also said the international internet had been blocked since the beginning of January for four months, and that public sentiment shifted from pre-war anti-regime protest energy to wartime solidarity after attacks on civilians and threats from Donald Trump.

prop_args.thesis: External military pressure strengthens the Iranian state in the short run by converting anti-regime sentiment into nationalist solidarity.
mechanisms: First, war collapses the distinction between 'the regime' and 'the nation'. This is because (1) ordinary Iranians can oppose the Islamic Republic in peacetime but still see foreign bombs as an attack on the country itself, (2) external threats create a common identity that overrides factional grievances, and (3) even anti-establishment citizens shift from protest mode to defense mode when they believe the homeland is under existential threat.

Second, bombardment creates a rally-around-the-flag effect that the regime can exploit. Three reasons: one, the state can present itself as the only organized actor capable of protecting civilians; two, public gatherings and visible solidarity become proof of legitimacy; three, the regime gains a propaganda narrative that foreign enemies, not domestic repression, are the immediate danger.

Third, the war buys the regime time to suppress dissent and postpone accountability. This matters because (1) protests become socially harder to sustain when people fear instability, (2) the public prioritizes survival and logistics over political mobilization, and (3) the state can use emergency conditions, internet controls, and security framing to delay any renewed uprising.

prop_args.thesis: Iran’s domestic resilience infrastructure makes coercive pressure less effective than expected and can even reduce the immediate humanitarian and political shock of sanctions or war.
mechanisms: First, the existence of a local intranet and domestic app ecosystem keeps basic life functioning under isolation. This is because (1) people can still hail taxis, order food, communicate, and access entertainment, (2) the economy has adapted around local substitutes like Rubika, Bale, Snapp!, Tapsi, and Digikala, and (3) partial continuity lowers the chance of total social breakdown.

Second, the state and society have learned to normalize wartime conditions. Three reasons: one, Tehran has historical memory of the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War and daily strikes; two, residents already relocate within the city rather than flee entirely; three, partial normalization reduces panic and mass displacement.

Third, selective pressure can backfire by hardening anti-American and anti-Israeli sentiment. This matters because (1) civilian casualties and infrastructure attacks make hostility feel personal rather than ideological, (2) Trump-style threats to erase Iran’s map or civilization intensify defiance, and (3) broader public resentment can strengthen long-term regime narratives about foreign encirclement.

opp_args.thesis: The apparent rally-around-the-flag effect is temporary and masks deeper structural fragility that will re-emerge once the war pressure eases.
mechanisms: First, wartime unity does not solve the underlying legitimacy crisis. One, the interview itself notes a deep rift between the system and society before the war; two, grievances over political representation, economic hardship, sanctions, and identity gaps remain unresolved; three, once the external threat recedes, those same grievances return with greater intensity.

Second, prolonged war and isolation worsen the material conditions that drive protest. One, the internet shutdown already lasts four months and blocks normal economic activity; two, water scarcity and economic pressure are described as building toward a breaking point; three, if the Strait of Hormuz blockade or wartime disruption continues, the regime will face inflation, shortages, and renewed street anger.

Third, repression plus nationalism can only defer, not eliminate, opposition. One, the state’s ability to manage solidarity is partly coercive and not fully voluntary; two, people may tolerate emergency conditions now but will resent the regime if it fails to deliver a new social contract; three, the article explicitly suggests the Islamic Republic may be facing one of its last chances to rebuild legitimacy.

opp_args.thesis: External attacks can radicalize the population against the regime’s enemies, but they also expose the regime’s inability to protect civilians and thereby undermine long-term trust.
mechanisms: First, visible civilian harm creates a competence test the state may fail. One, if people are bombed while gathering in squares with children, they may eventually ask why the government could not shield them; two, if attacks hit infrastructure and daily life, the regime is blamed for vulnerability; three, repeated exposure to insecurity can turn patriotic anger into demand for accountability.

Second, the war can widen the gap between elite narratives and lived reality. One, the regime may frame the conflict as national defense, but ordinary people experience shortages, internet restrictions, and fear; two, selective access to the intranet shows the state can control information but not solve material distress; three, when the emergency ends, people may compare the promised defense with the actual costs and turn back against the system.

Third, international escalation can create a stronger opposition coalition over time. One, war can unite anti-regime and anti-war constituencies around ending the conflict; two, economic pain from sanctions, blockade, and destruction broadens the base of discontent beyond activists; three, the more the regime ties itself to national survival, the more catastrophic any future failure becomes.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is timing: the article strongly supports a short-term rally-around-the-flag effect, but it also shows the underlying legitimacy and economic crisis is still there. Prop wins on immediate regime survival and protest suppression; Opp wins if the motion is about durable stability, because the same war that unifies society now can deepen the structural grievances that explode later.

cards.title: Europe Risks Replacing Gulf Energy Dependence With Chinese Clean-Tech Dependence
cards.region: Europe / China / Middle East (Strait of Hormuz)
cards.background: The article argues that the Iran war and tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have exposed Europe’s continued dependence on imported fossil fuels. Since the war began, the European Union has spent an additional €24 billion ($28 billion) on fossil-fuel imports, while the US oil and gas sector is set to gain at least $60 billion in windfall profits and Russia up to $100 billion in extra fiscal revenues. The piece says electricity now accounts for about 30% of China’s total energy consumption, versus roughly 20% in the US and Europe, and contrasts Spain’s wholesale power prices averaging €60/MWh with Italy’s near €130/MWh.

prop_args.thesis: Europe’s energy-security problem is no longer just oil and gas dependence; without massive electrification investment, it will simply swap one strategic dependency for another, this time on China.
mechanisms: First, electrification is the new source of strategic autonomy. This is because (1) low-cost domestic electricity directly lowers industrial costs and insulates economies from fossil-fuel shocks, (2) control over grids, storage, EVs, heat pumps, and renewables determines who can scale the next energy system, and (3) countries that move first lock in supply chains and standards that others must buy into.

Second, China is already ahead in the core chokepoints of the clean-energy economy. Three reasons: one, it has spent decades integrating mining, refining, batteries, EVs, and renewables into one system; two, it controls key critical-mineral and manufacturing bottlenecks; three, it has already electrified a much larger share of its economy, with electricity at roughly 30% of total energy use versus about 20% in Europe.

Third, Europe’s current policy mix is too weak to close the gap. This matters because (1) the EU’s new frameworks like the Net-Zero Industry Act and Critical Raw Materials Act are mostly regulatory, (2) the article explicitly says the financing gap is the main constraint and that current resources are insufficient, and (3) without common debt or large-scale industrial policy, Europe will remain exposed to imported fossil fuels in the short run and Chinese clean-tech dependence in the long run.

prop_args.thesis: The Iran shock proves that energy security is about resilience through domestic electrification, not just diversification of oil suppliers.
mechanisms: First, fossil-fuel markets create immediate macroeconomic vulnerability. This is because (1) disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz raise import bills, (2) higher energy costs feed inflation and keep interest rates elevated, and (3) Europe has already absorbed an extra €24 billion in fossil-fuel import costs since the war began.

Second, electrified systems are structurally more resilient than fuel-import systems. Three reasons: one, renewables have near-zero marginal fuel costs, so wholesale prices are less exposed to geopolitical shocks; two, domestic generation and storage reduce exposure to shipping chokepoints; three, grid-based systems can be scaled and localized faster than oil and gas supply chains can be re-routed.

Third, the distributional evidence inside Europe shows the model works. This matters because Spain’s renewables set wholesale prices about 80% of the time at around €60/MWh, while Italy’s gas dependence leaves it near €130/MWh, showing that electrification is not abstract ideology but a concrete buffer against price volatility.

opp_args.thesis: Europe is not doomed to Chinese dependence; with the right mix of regulation, procurement, and allied supply chains, it can build energy security without surrendering strategic autonomy.
mechanisms: First, Europe is already building the institutional architecture for industrial catch-up. One, the Net-Zero Industry Act, Critical Raw Materials Act, European Chips Act, and Industrial Accelerator Act all target bottlenecks in manufacturing and inputs; two, public procurement and state aid can create demand for European-made clean tech; three, trusted-supply-chain rules can reduce reliance on China without needing full autarky.

Second, dependence on China is not inevitable because supply chains are diversifiable. One, Europe can source minerals and components from multiple partners rather than one hegemon; two, the US, Japan, Korea, and other allies also want to de-risk China, creating coalition capacity; three, unlike oil, clean-tech supply chains are more modular and can be re-shored over time.

Third, the transition itself can reduce geopolitical exposure even if some inputs are imported. This matters because (1) once electrification infrastructure is built, marginal energy costs fall and fuel import bills shrink, (2) the biggest vulnerability in the article is fossil-fuel price shocks, not clean-tech imports, and (3) a temporary reliance on Chinese components is less strategically dangerous than permanent dependence on Gulf hydrocarbons.

opp_args.thesis: The article overstates China’s advantage because Europe’s problem is financing and coordination, not an inability to compete technologically.
mechanisms: First, Europe still has strong industrial and regulatory capabilities. One, it has the world’s largest single market, which can scale standards and demand; two, it already leads in climate regulation and can use that to shape global markets; three, its firms remain competitive in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and grid technology.

Second, the financing gap is politically solvable if the crisis deepens. One, energy shocks create public support for common borrowing and industrial policy; two, Eurobonds and EU-level investment can be justified as security spending; three, once governments treat electrification as strategic infrastructure, capital can be mobilized quickly.

Third, China’s lead may be less durable than it appears. One, its dominance in clean-tech supply chains creates overcapacity and trade backlash; two, other states can impose anti-dumping, local-content, and diversification policies; three, strategic dependence on China is politically more visible and therefore more likely to trigger countermeasures than dependence on diffuse fossil-fuel markets.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether energy security is defined by the source of power or by control over the next industrial system. Prop wins if the judge believes electrification is the new strategic terrain and that Europe’s financing gap makes Chinese dependence likely; opp wins if they frame Europe’s current problem as a solvable investment/coordination failure rather than a structural loss to China.

cards.title: UK Rail Renationalisation Tests Whether Public Ownership Can Fix Service Quality Without Cheaper Fares
cards.region: United Kingdom (West of England; South Wales)
cards.background: Great Western Railway (GWR), which runs services from London to the south-west of England and South Wales, will return to public ownership on 13 December. The operator is based in Swindon and has been running trains across the south-west for 20 years; its routes include Taunton, Bristol, Gloucester and other major stations. The Department for Transport says the move will bring passengers, rather than shareholders, to the heart of railways, while the transport secretary has warned that renationalisation will not necessarily lower fares. Wales nationalised rail services in 2021 and Scotland followed in 2022; several English operators, including Greater Anglia and South Western Railway, are already publicly owned.

prop_args.thesis: Renationalising GWR is the right move because it aligns incentives around service quality, network coordination, and long-term regional growth rather than short-term shareholder returns.
mechanisms: First, public ownership improves service planning and reliability. This is because (1) the operator no longer has to extract dividends or cut costs to satisfy private owners, (2) the DfT can coordinate timetables, staffing, and maintenance with a single public mandate, and (3) performance can be judged on punctuality and connectivity rather than profit margins.

Second, renationalisation enables better regional integration and infrastructure investment. Three reasons: one, the West of England and South Wales depend on rail as a growth corridor into Bristol and London; two, a public operator can prioritise frequency and network expansion even where routes are not immediately maximally profitable; three, it reduces fragmentation across operators and makes it easier to deliver cross-boundary services like the Bristol-Taunton-London corridor.

Third, this creates a stronger basis for equitable access and political accountability. This matters because passengers, local mayors, and devolved governments can pressure a public operator directly, whereas private franchises diffuse blame between ministers and shareholders; that makes it easier to justify service improvements like the mayor’s call for four trains an hour across the regional network.

opp_args.thesis: Renationalisation is mostly symbolic because ownership change does not solve the real constraints on fares, capacity, and infrastructure.
mechanisms: First, the biggest bottleneck is infrastructure, not ownership. One, rail punctuality and frequency depend on track capacity, signalling, and station upgrades, which are controlled by the wider state and require capital spending; two, the article itself notes the focus is on improving services and infrastructure rather than fares; three, if the network cannot physically support more trains, public ownership cannot magically create them.

Second, public ownership can reduce efficiency and weaken incentives. One, without competitive pressure or profit discipline, managers may face softer budget constraints and lower productivity; two, political interference can lead to decisions based on electoral optics rather than operational efficiency; three, if losses are socialised, there is a risk of chronic underperformance being tolerated rather than fixed.

Third, passengers may see little direct consumer benefit. One, the transport secretary has already warned renationalisation will not necessarily lower fares; two, if fares stay high and service improvements are slow, the public may pay more through taxes without getting cheaper tickets; three, that makes the reform vulnerable to being judged as a costly ownership swap rather than a substantive improvement.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether ownership itself changes outcomes or whether rail performance is mainly determined by infrastructure and state capacity. Prop wins if it proves coordination and accountability are the binding constraints; opp wins if it shows that the hard limits are capital-intensive and that renationalisation mostly changes who absorbs the losses.

THBT public ownership is preferable to private franchises for essential transport services
THP a world where regional rail networks are run by publicly owned operators
THBT governments should prioritise service quality over fare reductions in rail nationalisation

cards.title: US-Iran Maritime Escalation Turns the Strait of Hormuz Into a Coercive Blockade Contest
cards.region: Iran / United States / Strait of Hormuz / Gulf region
cards.background: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US of choosing a "reckless military adventure" instead of diplomacy, after both sides blamed each other for attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. The US said it fired on Iranian vessels and disabled two Iranian-flagged oil tankers on Friday, while Centcom said Iran launched missiles, drones, and small boats at three US warships. The confrontation comes as the US maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports and says more than 70 tankers are being prevented from entering or leaving Iranian ports; Trump said the ceasefire remains intact and Iran is expected to respond to US proposals on Friday.

prop_args.thesis: US coercive pressure is the only thing that can force Iran into a deal, because diplomacy without leverage would simply let Tehran buy time and keep escalating at sea.
mechanisms: First, blockade and maritime interdiction create immediate material pain. This is because (1) Iran depends on the Strait of Hormuz for export access and import flows, (2) the US can physically stop tankers from moving, and (3) that turns abstract sanctions into real revenue loss and domestic pressure on the regime.

Second, military pressure improves bargaining leverage by narrowing Iran’s options. Three reasons: one, it signals that continued proxy or naval attacks will be met with costs; two, it forces Iran to choose between escalation and compromise; three, it makes any future agreement more credible because Iran has already demonstrated it cannot simply ignore US demands.

Third, keeping the pressure on protects global energy markets from a worse shock later. This matters because if Iran is allowed to keep controlling or threatening the Strait, it can repeatedly weaponize the 20% of global oil and LNG that passes through it, so short-term coercion may prevent a longer, more destabilizing conflict over shipping.

opp_args.thesis: US military coercion is counterproductive because it hardens Iranian resolve, raises the risk of regional escalation, and gives Tehran incentives to weaponize the Strait of Hormuz further.
mechanisms: First, pressure strengthens Iranian hardliners and weakens moderates. One, when the US fires on tankers and blocks ports, Tehran can frame compromise as surrender; two, that reduces the domestic political space for any negotiator to accept concessions; three, it makes retaliation more likely because leaders need to prove they are not bowing to pressure.

Second, the blockade creates a classic escalation spiral in a chokepoint. One, the Strait of Hormuz is too strategically important for both sides to tolerate losses; two, every attack on ships or ports increases the chance of miscalculation involving US warships, tankers, and Gulf allies; three, once commercial shipping is disrupted, third parties get dragged in through energy price spikes and security commitments.

Third, coercion damages the US’s own strategic position by turning a bargaining problem into a credibility and alliance problem. One, allies in the Gulf and global markets see the US as unable to stabilize the waterway; two, prolonged disruption makes the US look like the actor responsible for higher oil prices and shipping insecurity; three, that reduces support for Washington’s terms and makes any eventual deal harder to sell.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercion produces compliance or escalation. The prop side wins if you think Iran is primarily responding to hard constraints and that only credible force can change its calculus; the opp side wins if you think the Strait of Hormuz is a classic escalation trap where pressure predictably increases retaliation and global spillovers.

THBT the US should prioritize coercive pressure over diplomacy in negotiations with Iran
THP a world where states can interdict shipping to enforce compliance with sanctions

cards.title: Ransomware Against Shared EdTech Infrastructure Turns Universities’ Digital Dependence Into a Systemic Vulnerability
cards.region: United States / Canada / Australia / Global education sector
cards.background: A cyber attack reportedly linked to the hacking group ShinyHunters disrupted Canvas, the academic software platform used by thousands of schools and universities across the US, Canada and Australia. Instructure, the owner of Canvas, said by late Thursday that the platform was 'available for most users', but several universities were still reporting outages on Friday. The article says the attack affected an estimated 9,000 institutions, with universities including the University of Sydney, Penn State, Mississippi State, the University of British Columbia, the University of Toronto, UCLA, the University of Chicago and Northwestern reporting disruptions, exam cancellations, or warnings to students.

prop_args.thesis: This attack proves that centralized education technology creates a single point of failure, so governments and institutions should reduce dependence on dominant private platforms.
mechanisms: First, platform concentration turns one breach into a sector-wide outage. This is because (1) thousands of institutions rely on the same vendor, (2) a compromise at the provider level instantly propagates across universities, and (3) schools cannot quickly substitute another system during exam season, so the operational shock is multiplied.

Second, the attack creates immediate academic and administrative harm that is hard to reverse. Three reasons: one, students miss submission deadlines and exams are postponed; two, universities must make ad hoc exceptions, which creates inconsistency and disputes; three, staff time shifts from teaching to crisis management, reducing institutional capacity at the worst possible moment.

Third, repeated attacks on shared infrastructure incentivize costly resilience reforms. This matters because institutions will be pushed toward redundancy, offline contingency planning, and stricter procurement standards, which reduces future systemic risk even if it raises short-term costs.

prop_args.thesis: Cyber extortion against universities is especially damaging because it exploits institutions that cannot credibly refuse payment or disruption.
mechanisms: First, universities face asymmetric pressure to restore access quickly. This is because (1) they are time-sensitive environments with exams, grading, and enrollment deadlines, (2) students and parents expect continuity, and (3) prolonged outages create reputational damage that can affect admissions and retention.

Second, the attack leverages sensitive data exposure as a coercive tool. Three reasons: one, the message reportedly threatened release of data; two, students and staff fear personal information leaks; three, institutions may be pushed into negotiations to avoid privacy and legal fallout.

Third, the incident normalizes ransom-based bargaining in the education sector. This matters because if attackers see that universities will face immediate pressure to settle, the sector becomes a repeat target, increasing the expected payoff of future attacks.

opp_args.thesis: The outage shows that private cloud and SaaS providers are still more resilient than fragmented in-house systems, so centralization can be efficient and ultimately safer.
mechanisms: First, a large vendor can patch and restore service faster than thousands of independent institutions. One, Instructure was able to bring Canvas back for most users within days; two, a centralized provider can deploy security fixes and incident response at scale; three, smaller universities would struggle to maintain equivalent cyber teams individually.

Second, shared platforms reduce total security costs across the sector. One, institutions avoid duplicating expensive infrastructure; two, vendors can invest more in specialized defenses than any single school; three, standardization makes monitoring and compliance easier than a patchwork of local systems.

Third, the fact that the attack was disruptive does not prove decentralization is better. One, many local systems would still be vulnerable to phishing and credential theft; two, fragmentation can create uneven security with weaker schools becoming easy targets; three, the real policy lesson is better vendor oversight, not abandoning scale.

opp_args.thesis: The main problem is not dependence on technology but inadequate cyber defense and contingency planning, so the correct response is regulation and preparedness rather than de-platforming.
mechanisms: First, institutions can preserve the benefits of digital learning while reducing harm through backups and offline procedures. One, exam extensions and manual submission channels can limit academic damage; two, universities can maintain parallel systems for critical functions; three, better incident drills reduce panic and confusion.

Second, the attack is a law-enforcement and governance failure more than a market-structure failure. One, the group reportedly sought ransom, so deterrence and prosecution matter; two, cross-border cybercrime requires state coordination; three, stronger breach reporting and threat intelligence sharing can reduce recurrence without dismantling efficient platforms.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether scale is a vulnerability or a source of resilience. Prop wins if the round is about systemic risk and the inability of institutions to absorb shocks during high-stakes periods; opp wins if they can show that centralized platforms are still the least-bad way to deliver secure, affordable education technology at scale.

THBT governments should require critical educational software to maintain offline redundancy and local backups
THP a world where universities are banned from outsourcing core academic infrastructure to a single vendor
THBT the state should regulate edtech platforms as critical infrastructure

cards.title: Democracies Begin Treating Chinese Transnational Repression as a Collective Security Threat
cards.region: United Kingdom / United States / Norway / China / Hong Kong
cards.background: On May 7, 2026, Peter Wai and Bill Yuen were convicted in the U.K. under the National Security Act for assisting a foreign intelligence service in what prosecutors described as a Chinese-linked "shadow policing operation." The same day, a U.S. trial continued against Liu Jianwang, who is charged with operating a secret Chinese police station in Manhattan’s Chinatown, while Norwegian authorities arrested a Chinese national accused of collecting sensitive data near Andøya Spaceport. The article argues these cases reflect a broader Chinese campaign of transnational repression targeting Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans, and other dissidents abroad.

prop_args.thesis: Democracies should respond to Chinese transnational repression with coordinated, alliance-based security tools rather than isolated domestic prosecutions.
mechanisms: First, coordination closes the jurisdictional gaps that Beijing exploits. This is because (1) repression networks are designed to operate across borders through embassies, trade offices, proxies, and diaspora informants, (2) unilateral enforcement lets operatives shift activity to the weakest legal system, and (3) shared watchlists, intelligence, and mutual legal assistance make it harder for Beijing to simply relocate the same operation from London to New York to Oslo.

Second, collective action raises the cost of repression and deters future operations. Three reasons: one, synchronized prosecutions and diplomatic expulsions signal that no single country can be singled out safely; two, public attribution reduces deniability for front organizations like HKETOs or covert police stations; three, the threat of coordinated sanctions and visa bans forces Chinese agencies to internalize the diplomatic cost of harassment campaigns.

Third, this protects diaspora communities more effectively than case-by-case law enforcement. This matters because (1) victims often do not trust local police until multiple states validate the threat, (2) intimidation is meant to silence political participation, so visible protection restores speech and organizing, and (3) if democracies fail to defend exiles on their soil, they create a chilling effect that weakens asylum, free expression, and the credibility of liberal citizenship itself.

opp_args.thesis: Treating transnational repression as a collective security issue risks over-securitizing ordinary diplomacy and producing backlash that makes enforcement less effective.
mechanisms: First, broad coordination can blur the line between legitimate foreign influence and espionage. One, states may overclassify benign diaspora activity as hostile interference; two, this creates civil liberties concerns for Chinese communities and other migrant groups; three, overreach reduces public trust and makes it harder to identify real covert operations.

Second, escalation can trigger retaliation against democracies and their citizens. One, Beijing can respond with arrests, trade pressure, or diplomatic expulsions; two, smaller states like Norway may be especially vulnerable to coercion and therefore less willing to cooperate; three, if the response is too confrontational, allies may prefer quiet case-by-case policing over a unified front.

Third, domestic legal tools may already be the best available response. One, prosecutions under national security, foreign agents, and surveillance laws are concrete and enforceable; two, alliance-wide frameworks are slow and politically difficult to operationalize; three, waiting for multilateral consensus can delay protection for victims who need immediate police action and court remedies.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether transnational repression is best understood as a set of isolated crimes or as a coordinated state strategy. Prop wins if it proves the latter, because the offense is structurally cross-border and therefore requires cross-border deterrence; Opp wins only if it can show that coordination meaningfully increases backlash or overreach enough to outweigh the security gains.
